Hysterectomy Hell

By: Catherine Rice | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
One in four women undergo a hysterectomy by the age of 55 years old, according to American statistics. In many cases, its unnecessary.

Unique Selling Point:
One in four women undergo a hysterectomy by the age of 55 years old. In some cases, its entirely unnecessary. A Cape Town woman, Melanie Verwoerd, has written a book and produced a podcast "Never Waste A Good Hysterectomy" detailing the trauma of her experiences.

Summary:
Melanie Verwoerd was diagnosed with an ovarian tumour in 2021. She was told that there was a 70 to 80% chance that it was cancerous and a radical hysterectomy was performed. Turned out, the tumour was benign, and she needn't have had a hysterectomy after all. Eight months of a gruelling recovery process followed. Hundreds of women have contacted her since her book was published, and her podcast broadcast, detailing their experiences. Verwoerd has become somewhat of an activist, urging women to obtain second opinions and spreading awareness about the difficult mental and physical recovery after a radical hysterectomy.

Further information:
Jeanne van Zyl is a 43 year old woman who had to undergo a radical hysterectomy because she had cervical cancer. What she had not prepared for, was the emotional and physical trauma she endured after the operation. Her mother came across Melanie's book and podcast, and she immediately got in touch. There is no real support for women going through this life changing procedure, but Melanie is trying to change that, by raising awareness and offering support to the many women who have contacted her since she published her own experiences. Jeanne went into surgery-induced menopause, which also complicated her recovery and she has since dealt with depression. Her operation was fairly recent, on March 30th. She has had to deal with night sweats, and must now take hormones. Furthermore, she didn't expect to feel such rage after the operation. But, talking to other women like Melanie, has helped in her recovery process. Jeanne's hysterectomy was unavoidable and life-saving, but she was not prepared for the gruelling recovery process and lack of support. Vernie Isaacs is still in pain after her radical hysterectomy on the 24th of April. She is a teacher and was booked off work for nine weeks. She believes there isn't enough preparation or support for women who have to have this life-changing procedure.

Script:


VO 1 The womb …. the starting point of life for all of us - but, if the womb is removed, in a surgical procedure called a hysterectomy, the consequences can be devastating… so why is it the second most common surgery for women, following cesareans?

PRESENTER LINK: (Clip 5869 / Day two) Hysterectomies can be vital interventions where medical emergencies call for them. But, shockingly sometimes they are done unnecessarily. So when is it essential and when can you ask your doctor for alternative treatments?

VO 2 When a woman has abnormal bleeding, uterine prolapse, fibroids or cancer - doctors most often recommend a hysterectomy… but research now suggests that as many as one in five may be unnecessary.

VO 3 When the surgery goes even further, removing the uterus, cervix, part of the vagina ….that’s a radical hysterectomy.

VO 4 For Melanie Verwoerd, it was the only option offered when a routine gynaecologist visit revealed an ovarian tumour. She had no symptoms… and no idea that her life was about to change dramatically.

UPSOUND Melanie Verwoerd Cip 5817 Day 1 Time code: 01:10 And it felt like my world just froze. Time code 01:20 Originally, I was told there was a 70 to 80% chance it would be cancer.

VO 5 It was only after surgery, that she discovered her tumour had in fact been benign.

UPSOUND Melanie Verwoerd Day One Clip 5818 Time code 12:16 The doctor had asked permission to take photographs of what they took out. And I looked at it a few nights after the op. And it really upset me to see it. To see my uterus, my cervix, my ovaries and on the one side this huge growth. To think that was where my children were conceived in and grew in.

VO 6 Melanie was not prepared for the difficult recovery process and she found there was little support available.

UPSOUND Melanie Verwoerd Clip 5818 Day 1 Time code: 08:33 So painful, so painful, I’ve had medical things done, had two caesareans, nothing can compare to the incredible invasion and the pain you experience.

VO 7 Like most women, Melanie was told she’d recover in four to six weeks - but that turned into a gruelling six-month ordeal and an emotional rollercoaster.

UPSOUND ERIN Clip 5818 Time code: 14:08 In that mix of emotions where does anger and rage fit in?

UPSOUND Melanie Verwoerd Clip 5819 Time code: 00:17 The surgeon said to me in hospital that one of the side effects of a radical hysterectomy can be a complete loss of libido and I flew into him and said yes if this was a man you wouldn’t say that so glibly. But, the real fury and anger came a few weeks later when I thought about all these women who are abandoned post hysterectomy in terms of support from the medical profession and have to suffer on their own. Cip 5818 Time code: 15:04 It was red hot rage and led me to do a lot of research.

VO 7a. Melanie came to the disturbing conclusion that when it comes to cancer in women, far less research money goes to those that affect older women. In other words, removing the womb, is easier than finding better ways of diagnosing cancer.

UPSOUND Melanie Verwoerd Clip 5820 Day one Time code: 17:41
I think there is still subconsciously an attitude in society that once women have done their child bearing age, they become less visible, less important in our society. Because your main role is to have the babies and that’s done now. Time code 18:14 I think that definitely plays a role in hysterectomies.

VO 8 Melanie, a lifelong advocate for justice, now raises her voice to spread awareness about the potential harm of this procedure.

VO 9 Gynaecologist Dr Stefanie Hinz says there is sometimes only one way to diagnose ovarian cancer - AND THAT’S DOING a HYSTERECTOMY and removing the ovaries.

UPSOUND Dr Stephi Hinz Clip 5844 Day Two Time code: 15:38 But that also means you overtreat it sometimes. … 25:14 Thirty to forty percent of hysterectomies are done for fibroids and menoragia which is heavy periods, now there are plenty of other options.

VO 10 So.. if surgery to remove the uterus can be avoided, it should be.

ERIN Clip 5845 Day Two Time Code: 02:10 When would you say a hysterectomy is either reckless or simply unnecessary?

UPSPOUND Dr Steffi Hinz 02:17 Its relatively simple, if there are valid equally effective alternatives, you shouldn’t operate.

VO 11 There are no statistics in South Africa on the rate of women sent for hysterectomies. In the United States one in four will have one before the age of 55.

UPSOUND Dr Stefanie Hinz Clip 5844 Time code An absolute necessity is only give in two particular instances Time code 02:35 You must remember that most hysterectomies are done for quality of life. And quality of life is up to the patient, not the doctor. Like if anaemic periods.. Time code 3:00 So the absolute necessities are life saving, two areas, oncology and cancer surgery. Time code 3:29 The other field is obstetrical hysterectomy but this is basically patient who has baby and suffers haemmorage after birth.

VO 12 But even where a hysterectomy is still called for, the toll taken can be severe and unexpected. Menopause, the natural process in which a woman’s menstrual cycle ends and fertility declines, generally starts between the ages of 45 and 55 and sometimes takes years. But, removing the ovaries immediately triggers menopause.

UPSOUND Dr Stephi Hinz / Gynaecologist Clip 5844 Time code 18:14 Surgical menopause aint nice because you’re basically dropping your hormone levels to zero in twenty four hours. And its a process that otherwise is stretched out over years and years.

VO 13 That’s what happened to Jeanne van Zyl, diagnosed with cervical cancer …who underwent a radical hysterectomy that triggered menopause at the age of 43.

UPSOUND Jeanne van Zyl Clip 5811 Time code 04:15 Six months ago I was perfectly fine and healthy. 04:45 This came out of the blue, I really battle with it. It’s hot flushes. .feeling older than I should.

VO 13a It also meant her dream of having a child was shattered.

UPSOUND Jeanne van Zyl / Clip 5808 Time code 11:38 I’ve always wanted to have children, and that was such a big OK its really not going to happen. (shots at park from Day Two, empty swings etc). Clip 5811 Time code 04:37 You know its your womanhood. I wanted to cling to that a little longer before I let it go.

VO 13b With hot flushes, cold sweats and depression, surgically-triggered menopause intensified her grief

UPSOUND Jeanne van Zyl Clip 5811 / Day One Time code 01:54 First, I was scared I was going to die and then I was scared I wasn’t going to die because I just didn’t want to go on anymore.

VO 14 Teacher and mother, Vernie Isaacs’s radical hysterectomy in April to treat an enlarged uterus and growths called fibroids, also triggered menopause.

UPSOUND Vernie van Zyl Time code 19:54 There was no way I could drive, there was no way I could raise my hand to write.

Erin: Day Two Clip 5902 Time code 10:46 In terms of the consequences, were you adequately prepared?

UPSOUND Vernie Isaacs I had no idea what I’m going to have to deal with after this operation. 15:25 I had these hot flushes, attacks, I was literally shivering. Add back in “my emotions were all over the place”

VO 15 And she too experienced an intense feeling of loss.

UPSOUND Vernie Isaacs Time code 28:58
these are the very organs that gave me the joy and the happiness of my life.

VO 16 Where possible, Dr Hinz advocates for less invasive techniques like keyhole surgery with shorter recovery times… when that’s an option.

VO 17 And when it’s not… Melanie believes doctors must prepare women for the emotional and physical toll of a hysterectomy. She has become a source of emotional support to Vernie, and many other women.

UPSOUND Melanie Verwoerd Time code 11:18 It’s cruel. It’s incredibly cruel I think
if doctors don’t help women, and often don’t even prepare them for how bad its going to be. Time code: 11:14 It’s one of the things that really needs to stop.
Make sure you see your test results. 19:30 Do not let doctors fob you off. Make sure you feel empowered and strong going into your medical journey.
